meta.theme: obedience to law explained by the acknowledged standing of the body issuing a demand rather than by the price of disobeying it, supported by an expected penalty too small to produce the observed compliance, by falls and rises that track fairness while enforcement stands still, and by obedience to rules the obedient think mistaken, with the sanction granted a constituent role and refused a motivating one

meta.reviewer_notes: A thesis with three supports and a final paragraph that gives the rejected account two things before refusing it a third, which is what keeps the attitude question genuinely hard: the author is neither hostile nor neutral but demoting. The EXCEPT question is built from the three supports plus a fourth claim that is plausible in the world and absent from the page.
meta.tone: confident, demoting rather than hostile, admonitory at the close

quality.adversarial_review: Q1's live rival is the option calling the passage a warning about the cost of enforcement, which is the last sentence of the last paragraph offered as the whole; the warning is a consequence drawn after the thesis has been argued for over three paragraphs of support. Q2's rival is the option that procedure matters more than substance, which invents a comparison the passage never makes, since the point of the unchanged penalties is that one variable moved and the other did not, not that one variable outranks the third. Q3's rival is the even-handed reading, which four paragraphs of controlled exposition invite and which the fifth destroys by assigning deterrence a bounded territory and refusing it an explanation. Q4's rival is the option about severity and rates of offending, which is exactly the sort of evidence the thesis would welcome and which the passage never offers, its arithmetic being about the chance of detection rather than about how harshly anything is punished.

paragraphs.text: Why do people obey the law? The answer that arrives first is the one a child would give: because of what happens if you do not. On that account a legal system is a machine for making disobedience expensive, and a citizen is a calculator who has worked out that the fine exceeds the gain. The account is not absurd and it is not sufficient. What is defended here is that most compliance, most of the time, rests on something the calculator has no room for, namely whether the body issuing the demand is taken to be entitled to issue it.

Begin with the arithmetic, which is the deterrent account's own ground. For the great majority of everyday rules, what is declared on a form, how fast a car is driven on an empty road at night, what becomes of a parking notice in a street without wardens, the chance of detection is small and is widely known to be small, and the penalty discounted by that chance comes to very little. Compliance in those cases is nevertheless high. A theory that explains obedience by price has to account for a rate of obedience that its own numbers cannot produce.

Then the exceptions, which fall in a pattern. Compliance drops where an authority is believed to have behaved unfairly, where a decision was taken without hearing anybody, or where a rule is pressed against one part of a population and not another, and it drops although nothing whatever has changed about the penalties or about the chance of being caught. It rises where procedures are made fairer, and again the penalties stand exactly where they were. What varies is not the price.

The third support is that the thing being responded to is narrower than agreement. People are not asking whether the rule is a good one. They keep rules they believe to be mistaken, and say so while keeping them. What is judged is the standing of the body that issued the rule and the manner of its issuing: whether it was entitled to decide, and whether it decided in a way that treated those bound by it as parties rather than as material. Obedience of this kind is owed to an office and not to an opinion.

None of this makes deterrence a myth. It works, and it works exactly where the other thing has failed or was never established: on the persistently predatory, on those who stand outside the arrangement and know it, and in the moments when the authority of a rule is in open dispute. Something stronger should be granted as well. A demand backed by no penalty at all is not a legal demand but a request, so the sanction is part of what makes the thing obeyed a law. What the grant does not license is the deterrent account's own claim, that the penalty is why the demand is met. A penalty can be a constituent of a demand without being the motive for meeting it. And there is a bill at the end of this. Legitimacy is cheap and enforcement is dear, so an authority that spends the first will find the cost of the second arriving in a form it cannot pay.

questions.target_mistake: characterising the passage by its closing warning or by its sharpest phrase, rather than by the claim that three paragraphs of support were assembled to establish
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say in a verb and an object: it argues that obedience runs on entitlement, and assigns the penalty a smaller job than the rival account gives it.
questions.stem: The passage is best characterised as

options.A: a demonstration that the threat of punishment has no part in securing obedience, and that legal systems could dispense with it
options.B: a survey of the reasons that people give when they are asked why they obey the law they live under
options.C: an argument that compliance runs chiefly on acknowledged standing, with punishment left the work that standing has failed to do
options.D: a warning that authorities which act unfairly face enforcement costs they cannot meet, and of where the warning ceases to apply

explanation.expert_notice: The first paragraph states a thesis in a single clause, that compliance rests on whether the body issuing a demand is taken to be entitled to issue it. Three paragraphs of support follow in order, and the fifth assigns deterrence a territory of its own: the persistently predatory, the outsiders, and the moments when a rule's authority is disputed.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option carries the thesis and the demotion together, which is what the shape of the passage requires. Every paragraph is doing work under it: the arithmetic shows the price cannot produce the observed compliance, the exceptions show what does move it, the third support narrows what is being judged, and the last paragraph hands the sanction the residue. A characterisation that removes either half leaves a paragraph unexplained.
explanation.question_type_note: Best characterisation asks for the passage's move in a verb and an object, and both have to survive the final paragraph. Concessions made there are part of the move, not exceptions to it.
explanation.reading_habit: When an author states a thesis and then spends paragraphs numbering his supports, characterise the passage by the thesis rather than by the most striking sentence in it. Memorable lines are usually consequences.

distractors.why_wrong: The fifth paragraph refuses this twice over, saying deterrence is not a myth and that a demand with no penalty behind it is a request rather than a law, which is the opposite of a system that could dispense with it. The claim being made is about what explains compliance, not about whether punishment has any part in the business.
distractors.seductive_element: Three paragraphs are spent showing that price cannot account for obedience, and a reader keeping the direction rather than the degree will arrive at the stronger version.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing here reports what anybody says about their own motives. The evidence is about rates of compliance under varying conditions, and the one remark about people saying something concerns their saying a rule is mistaken while keeping it.
distractors.seductive_element: Legitimacy is a term about how people regard an authority, which sounds like something established by asking them.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the last sentence of the passage, drawn as a consequence once the argument is complete, and no boundary is ever set to it. Offered as the characterisation it makes the three supports look like preliminaries to a piece of advice the author gives in a single line.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because it is the passage's final and most quotable thought, and closing sentences are often where a thesis is restated.

questions.target_mistake: reading the evidence about unchanged penalties as a ranking of procedure against substance, rather than as the isolation of one variable
questions.prediction_target: The learner should predict that the answer will be about what the unchanged penalty rules out, which is the rival explanation of the movement.
questions.stem: It can be inferred that the author treats a rise in compliance after a reform of procedure, with penalties unchanged, as significant because it

options.A: shows that people are more frightened of unfair authorities than of fair ones
options.B: separates the two candidate causes, since only one of them has moved
options.C: demonstrates that procedure matters more to people than the substance of the rules does
options.D: proves that the penalties attached to those rules had never been enforced at all

explanation.expert_notice: The third paragraph is built around a single design. Compliance falls when fairness falls and rises when fairness rises, and in both directions the passage repeats that nothing has changed about the penalties or the chance of being caught. The paragraph then states the point in four words: what varies is not the price.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option names why that design matters. Two explanations are on offer, price and standing, and the observation holds one of them fixed while the other moves, so the movement cannot be attributed to the one that stayed still. This is why the author bothers to say twice that the penalties stand where they were, a detail that would be pointless in a passage merely reporting that fairness is popular.
explanation.question_type_note: An inference question about evidence asks what the evidence rules out. Look for the variable the author insists has not changed.
explanation.reading_habit: When a writer repeats that something stayed the same, treat the repetition as the argument rather than as padding. He is telling you which explanation the observation eliminates.

distractors.why_wrong: Fear is the rival account's currency, and the observation is offered to show that fear is not what moved. The passage also has compliance falling rather than rising when an authority behaves unfairly, which is the reverse of what this option describes.
distractors.seductive_element: It keeps the passage's own vocabulary of unfairness and compliance, and a reader who has not fixed the direction of the movement can assemble it either way.

distractors.why_wrong: No comparison between procedure and substance is made anywhere. The fourth paragraph says people obey rules they believe to be mistaken, which separates standing from agreement, and it never ranks the two as sources of compliance.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the passage does insist that people are not judging the merits of the rule, and a reader may convert that separation into a hierarchy.

distractors.why_wrong: Nothing is claimed about non-enforcement. The second paragraph's point is that the chance of detection is small and known to be small, which is a statement about probability rather than about a penalty that was never applied at all.
distractors.seductive_element: The arithmetic paragraph really does describe rules that go largely unpoliced, and the step from rarely enforced to never enforced is a short one to take carelessly.

questions.target_mistake: mistaking four paragraphs of controlled argument against a position for either hostility to it or neutrality between it and its rival
questions.prediction_target: The learner should be able to say: he keeps deterrence, assigns it a bounded territory, and takes away from it the thing it claims to explain.
questions.stem: The author's attitude towards the deterrent account of obedience is best described as

options.A: sceptical of its evidence, which though careful is drawn from unrepresentative offences
options.B: even-handed, treating it and its rival as two descriptions of the same facts, neither complete
options.C: hostile, since he holds that punishment corrupts the relation between a citizen and the law
options.D: willing to grant it a real and limited job, while denying it the explanation it claims for itself

explanation.expert_notice: The fifth paragraph does the tonal work in three moves. Deterrence is not a myth and has a named territory; the sanction is granted a constituent role, since a demand with no penalty is a request; and then the account's own claim, that the penalty is why the demand is met, is refused in the next sentence.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option keeps all three. The author is not attacking deterrence but demoting it, which is a distinct attitude: he expands what it is owed at one point, granting more than its defenders usually ask, and removes from it the explanatory role that is the whole of its ambition. An option that makes him hostile has to account for the grant, and one that makes him neutral has to account for the refusal.
explanation.question_type_note: Attitude is two decisions, valence and intensity, and an author who gives a position something before taking something away has fixed both in one paragraph.
explanation.reading_habit: Find the sentence where a writer concedes to the view he is arguing against. It sets the ceiling on how hostile any correct attitude option can be, and it is usually near the end.

distractors.why_wrong: The evidence of the deterrent account is never questioned. Its arithmetic is accepted and used, the second paragraph calling it the account's own ground and then showing that the numbers cannot produce the compliance observed.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the second paragraph does look like an attack on the other side's data, and readers expect an argument against a theory to begin by doubting its facts.

distractors.why_wrong: The author decides throughout. He states a thesis in the first paragraph, marshals three supports for it, and assigns the rival account a residue, which is a verdict rather than a pair of incomplete descriptions.
distractors.seductive_element: The prose is calm and gives the other side both a territory and a constituent role, and evenhandedness is habitually mistaken for having no position.

distractors.why_wrong: No corruption of any relation is alleged. The passage says a penalty is part of what makes an obeyed thing a law, which is the opposite of treating punishment as something that spoils the citizen's relation to it.
distractors.seductive_element: A passage that takes obedience away from fear and gives it to entitlement sounds as though it must disapprove of fear, and readers supply the moral colouring.

questions.target_mistake: accepting a claim that the thesis would welcome as one the passage actually made, because it belongs to the same argument in the world outside the text
questions.stem: The passage offers each of the following in support of its thesis EXCEPT:

options.A: Where an authority raises the penalties attached to a rule, compliance with it does not improve, or improves only briefly.
options.B: People keep rules they believe to be mistaken, which shows that what is asked for is not agreement.
options.C: Compliance falls where an authority is thought to have behaved unfairly, although enforcement has not changed.
options.D: For many everyday rules the penalty, discounted by the chance of being caught, comes to very little, and compliance is high all the same.

explanation.expert_notice: The three supports are announced and separated: the arithmetic in the second paragraph, the patterned exceptions in the third, and the narrowness of what is being judged in the fourth. In every one of them the penalties are held still, and the passage never once describes a case in which they move.
explanation.correct_reasoning: The correct option is the one support the passage does not use, and the hedge at its end does not make it any more present. The arithmetic turns on the chance of detection rather than on the size of a penalty, and the comparisons hold the penalties fixed while the fairness of procedure moves; nowhere is there a case in which penalties rise at all. A claim of that kind would be welcome evidence for the thesis, which is why its absence is easy to miss.
explanation.question_type_note: On an EXCEPT question, find the three that are in the passage; the answer is what remains, and it is usually plausible in the world rather than visibly false.
explanation.reading_habit: When an option would help the author's case, check twice that he made it. Arguments attract familiar supporting facts, and readers remember the argument's neighbourhood rather than its text.

distractors.why_wrong: The fourth paragraph states both the fact and the conclusion drawn from it, saying people keep rules they believe mistaken and that what is judged is the standing of the issuing body rather than the merits of the rule.
distractors.seductive_element: The second clause reads as an inference a candidate has supplied, and options that appear to reason feel less like quotations than options that merely report.

distractors.why_wrong: The third paragraph asserts exactly this, and the clause about unchanged enforcement is the author's own, repeated in both directions so that the falls and the rises alike are shown to occur with the penalties standing where they were.
distractors.seductive_element: The qualification looks like the kind of condition an option writer adds to make a true statement false, and readers grow suspicious of clauses that do too much work.

distractors.why_wrong: This is the second paragraph compressed. The chance of detection is small and known to be small, the penalty discounted by that chance comes to very little, and compliance is nevertheless high, which is the whole of the first support.
distractors.seductive_element: It is the live rival, because the arithmetic is stated across several sentences rather than in one, so a reader matching phrases will not find it whole anywhere.

mentor.challenge: A familiar explanation is not destroyed but moved to a smaller room. Watch the last paragraph, where the author gives the other side more than it asks for and then removes the one thing it wants, because the attitude question turns entirely on that sequence.
mentor.one_sentence_summary: Obedience to law is usually explained by the price of disobeying, and the price is too small in most everyday cases to produce the compliance actually observed, while compliance rises and falls with the fairness of an authority though the penalties never move, and people keep rules they think mistaken, so what is being answered is a body's entitlement to demand rather than a calculation about punishment, which leaves the sanction a real but bounded job and leaves an authority that squanders its standing with an enforcement bill it cannot pay.
mentor.main_idea: The commonest account of obedience says people comply because disobedience costs. For most everyday rules the expected cost is tiny and known to be tiny, and compliance is high anyway. Compliance also moves with the perceived fairness of the authority while the penalties stay fixed, and people obey rules they think are wrong. So what is being answered is whether the body issuing the demand is entitled to issue it. Deterrence still has real work, with predators, outsiders and disputed rules, and a penalty is part of what makes a demand legal, but it is not why most demands are met.
mentor.simple_explanation:
Why do people obey laws? The first answer anybody gives is: because of what happens if you don't. On that picture, the legal system is a machine that makes breaking the rules expensive, and each of us is doing a quick sum about fines and the chance of being caught.

The author says that picture is not silly, but it cannot be the main story. Here is his case, in three parts.

First, the arithmetic, which is the other side's own ground. Think about most ordinary rules: what you write on a form, how fast you drive on an empty road at night, what you do with a parking ticket in a street with no wardens. The chance of getting caught is small, everybody knows it is small, and once you multiply the penalty by that small chance you get almost nothing. And yet most people comply. A theory that explains obedience by price has to explain a level of obedience its own numbers cannot produce.

Second, look at when obedience breaks down. It drops when people believe an authority has behaved unfairly, when decisions are made without listening to anyone, or when a rule is enforced against one group and not another. And it drops even though nothing at all has changed about the punishment or the chance of being caught. It goes back up when procedures are made fairer, and again the punishments are exactly where they were. So the thing that is moving is not the price.

Third, notice what people are actually reacting to. It is not whether they agree with the rule. People follow rules they think are wrong, and will tell you they think they are wrong while following them. What they are judging is whether the body that made the rule had the standing to make it, and whether it went about it in a way that treated them as people with a stake rather than as things to be processed.

Then the author is careful. He does not say punishment is a myth. It works, and it works exactly where the other thing has failed or never existed: with people who live by preying on others, with people who are outside the arrangement and know it, and in moments when a rule's authority is genuinely in dispute. He gives the other side something more, in fact: a demand with no penalty behind it at all is not a law, it is a request. So the penalty is part of what makes the thing a law.

But, he says, that is not the same as saying the penalty is why anyone obeys. Something can be part of what a thing is without being the reason people do it.

And he ends with a warning. Standing is cheap and enforcement is expensive. An authority that spends its standing will find the bill for enforcement arriving in a form it cannot pay.
mentor.why_difficult: The passage argues against a position without ever becoming hostile to it, and readers who track direction rather than degree finish holding a stronger claim than the author makes, which the last paragraph refuses twice. The second difficulty is that the last paragraph gives the rejected account more than its defenders usually claim, making a penalty part of what a law is, and then withholds the thing they actually want, so the attitude is neither approval nor rejection but demotion. The third is the third paragraph, whose force lies in a clause about what did not change, which is easy to read as padding.
mentor.author_intention: To take the explanation of obedience away from calculation and give it to entitlement, while leaving the sanction a job precise enough that nobody can accuse him of pretending law works without it, and then to make the reader feel the cost of squandering the cheaper resource.

paragraph_journey.note: The obvious answer is fear of the penalty. That is not enough. Most obedience turns on whether the body demanding is thought entitled to demand.
For ordinary rules the chance of being caught is tiny, so the expected penalty is tiny, and compliance is high anyway.
Obedience falls with unfairness and rises with fairer procedure, while the penalties never move at all. So the price is not what changes.
Not whether the rule is good. People keep rules they think mistaken. What is judged is standing and manner.
Deterrence keeps real territory and even becomes part of what a law is. It still does not explain why most people comply. And squandered standing arrives later as an enforcement bill.

mentor.tone_progression: It opens almost casually, with the child's answer, hardens into confident argument through the three supports, becomes scrupulous in the last paragraph as the rival is given territory and then a constituent role, and finishes admonitory, with a warning delivered in the flattest possible language.
key_transitions: 'The account is not absurd and it is not sufficient.' (paragraph 1) — the rival is kept and demoted in a single sentence.
'What varies is not the price.' (close of paragraph 3) — the evidence of the whole paragraph is compressed into five words.
'A penalty can be a constituent of a demand without being the motive for meeting it.' (paragraph 5) — the grant and its limit stated together.
mentor.misunderstanding: The common wrong model is that the passage says punishment does not matter, which the last paragraph denies in two separate sentences, one giving deterrence a territory and one making the sanction part of what a law is. The opposite wrong model reads the same paragraph's generosity as neutrality and comes away thinking the author declines to choose, although he states a thesis in his first paragraph and spends three more establishing it. The passage is built out of an argument plus a concession, and readers keep one or the other rather than both.
mentor.traps_summary: This set offers the closing warning as the characterisation, the destruction of deterrence as the thesis, a ranking of procedure against substance in place of the isolation of a variable, neutrality in place of demotion, and a piece of evidence the argument would have welcomed and never used. Sorting each option into thesis, support, grant or warning answers all four.
mentor.reading_lesson: When an author argues against an explanation, find the paragraph where he says what the explanation still accounts for, because the correct answers to characterisation and attitude questions both live in the distance between demoting a view and destroying it. The companion habit is to treat any clause insisting that something did not change as the heart of the evidence: it is there to eliminate a rival cause, and options that ignore it will read the observation as a mere correlation or as a ranking.
mentor.real_world: The same division runs through every arrangement that relies on voluntary compliance: tax that is mostly self-assessed, safety rules on a site nobody inspects, a professional code enforced by a body with few investigators, the rules of a queue. Wherever inspection is thin and compliance is high, the cheap resource is doing the work, and its exhaustion shows up first as an enforcement budget that will not stretch.
mentor.takeaway: Authority that is believed costs almost nothing; authority that has to be enforced is priced by the hour.
mentor.reflection_question: Which rules do you follow without once thinking about what would happen if you did not, and what would have to change for you to start thinking about it?
